title: HTTP & REST deep dive
summary: Learn how HTTP requests, methods, status codes, and REST conventions let your code talk to web APIs.
objectives: Explain the request/response cycle behind every web API call
Use the core HTTP methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE correctly
Read status codes and headers to tell success from failure
Describe what makes an API RESTful, including resources and statelessness
Send authenticated requests with headers and an API key or token
Call a real JSON API from Python using the requests library

quiz.q: Which HTTP method should you use to fetch data without changing anything on the server?
quiz.why: GET retrieves a resource and is safe and read-only — it should never modify server state.

quiz.q: What does a 404 status code mean?
quiz.why: 404 is in the 4xx client-error family and means the requested resource does not exist at that URL.

quiz.q: Which status code family means the request succeeded?
quiz.why: 2xx codes (like 200 OK and 201 Created) signal success; 4xx is client error and 5xx is server error.

quiz.q: Name one property that makes an API RESTful.
quiz.answer: Statelessness — each request carries all the information needed and the server stores no client session between requests (also acceptable: resource-based URLs, standard HTTP methods).
quiz.why: REST treats data as resources addressed by URLs, uses standard HTTP methods, and is stateless so requests are independent.

quiz.q: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
quiz.answer: PUT replaces the entire resource with the data you send; PATCH updates only the specific fields you include.
quiz.why: Use PUT for a full replacement and PATCH for a partial update of an existing resource.

quiz.q: Where do you usually put an API key or token when calling a protected endpoint?
quiz.why: Credentials normally travel in a header such as Authorization: Bearer <token>, not in the visible path.

body_markdown:
## The request/response cycle

Every time your code talks to a web API, it follows the same pattern: a **client** sends a **request** to a **server**, and the server sends back a **response**. This is the heart of HTTP — the HyperText Transfer Protocol.

A request has four parts: a **method** (the verb), a **URL** (which resource), **headers** (metadata), and an optional **body** (data you send). A response comes back with a **status code**, headers, and usually a body — often JSON.

## HTTP methods (the verbs)

The method tells the server what you want to do with a resource.

- **GET** — read a resource. Safe and read-only.
- **POST** — create a new resource.
- **PUT** — replace an existing resource entirely.
- **PATCH** — update part of a resource.
- **DELETE** — remove a resource.

GET should never change anything. POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE are the ones that modify state.

## Status codes

The server replies with a three-digit code grouped into families:

- **2xx** — success (200 OK, 201 Created).
- **3xx** — redirection.
- **4xx** — client error — *you* sent something wrong (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found).
- **5xx** — server error — the server broke (500 Internal Server Error).

Always check the status code before trusting the body.

## What makes an API RESTful

**REST** is a set of conventions, not a technology. A RESTful API treats your data as **resources**, each with its own URL — for example `/users/42`. You act on those resources using the standard HTTP methods, and the API is **stateless**: every request carries everything the server needs, so the server keeps no memory of you between calls.

This is why REST scales well and feels predictable: `GET /users/42` always means the same thing.

## Calling an API from Python

The `requests` library makes HTTP calls simple. Install it first:

```bash
pip install requests
```

Then send a GET request and read the JSON response:

```python
import requests

r = requests.get("https://api.github.com/users/octocat")
print(r.status_code)        # 200
data = r.json()             # parse JSON into a dict
print(data["name"])         # The Octocat
```

To send data and authenticate, use a method with a body and an Authorization header:

```python
import requests

headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_TOKEN"}
payload = {"title": "Hello", "body": "My first API call"}
r = requests.post("https://api.example.com/posts",
                  json=payload, headers=headers)
print(r.status_code)        # 201 if created
```

## Your task

Use `requests` to call a free public API (try the GitHub users endpoint), print the status code, and pull two fields out of the JSON response.

slides.narration: Welcome back to Month Two. So far you've worked with data and S Q L. In this lesson we open the door to the wider web by learning H T T P and REST. These are the rules that let your code request data from any web A P I on the planet. By the end you'll understand the request and response cycle, the H T T P methods, status codes, and how to call a real A P I from Python.

slides.title: The request/response cycle
bullets: A client sends a request to a server.
The server sends back a response.
Both travel over H T T P.
This powers every web A P I call.
slides.narration: Everything starts with one simple pattern. Your code, the client, sends a request to a server. The server does some work and sends back a response. This conversation travels over H T T P, the HyperText Transfer Protocol. Every single web A P I call you ever make follows this same back and forth.

slides.title: Anatomy of a request
bullets: Method: the verb, like GET or POST.
U R L: which resource you want.
Headers: extra metadata.
Body: optional data you send.
slides.narration: Let's break a request into its parts. First, the method, which is the verb describing what you want to do. Second, the U R L, which says which resource you're after. Third, headers, which carry extra information like your credentials or the data format. And fourth, an optional body, which holds data you're sending up to the server.

slides.title: HTTP methods
bullets: GET reads a resource, safely.
POST creates a new resource.
PUT replaces; PATCH updates part.
DELETE removes a resource.
slides.narration: The method is the verb. GET reads a resource and should never change anything. POST creates something new. PUT replaces an entire resource, while PATCH updates just part of it. And DELETE removes a resource. Remember: GET is read-only, and the others are the ones that change things on the server.

slides.title: Status codes
bullets: 2 x x means success.
4 x x means you made a mistake.
5 x x means the server broke.
Check the code before the body.
slides.narration: Every response comes back with a three digit status code, grouped into families. Two x x means success. Three x x is redirection. Four x x means the client, that's you, sent something wrong, like a 404 Not Found. And five x x means the server itself failed. The golden rule: always check the status code before you trust the body.

slides.title: What makes it RESTful
bullets: Data is modelled as resources.
Each resource has its own U R L.
Use standard H T T P methods.
Stateless: every request stands alone.
slides.narration: REST is not a technology, it's a set of conventions. A RESTful A P I treats your data as resources, and each resource gets its own U R L, like slash users slash forty two. You act on them using the standard H T T P methods. And crucially, it's stateless: every request carries everything the server needs, so the server keeps no memory of you between calls. That's what makes REST predictable and scalable.

slides.title: Calling an API in Python
bullets: The requests library makes this easy.
Install it with pip first.
GET returns a response object.
Read JSON with r dot json.
slides.code:
import requests

r = requests.get(
  "https://api.github.com/users/octocat")
print(r.status_code)   # 200
data = r.json()
print(data["name"])    # The Octocat
slides.narration: Now let's make a real call. Python's requests library makes this beautifully simple. After installing it with pip, you call requests dot get with a U R L. You get back a response object. Check r dot status code to confirm it worked, then call r dot json to turn the Jason body into a Python dictionary you can read.

slides.title: Sending data & auth
bullets: POST sends data in the body.
Pass a dict with json equals payload.
Auth goes in a header.
Bearer token is the common pattern.
slides.narration: To send data, use POST and pass a Python dictionary through the json argument. The requests library turns it into Jason for you. To prove who you are, you add an Authorization header, usually the word Bearer followed by your token. A 201 status code tells you the resource was created successfully.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Using GET to change data.
Ignoring the status code.
Forgetting the auth header.
Putting your token in the U R L.
slides.narration: Let's flag the traps. One: using GET when you mean to change data. Two: ignoring the status code and assuming success. Three: forgetting the Authorization header on a protected endpoint, which gives you a 401. And four: putting your secret token in the visible U R L instead of a header. Avoid these and your A P I calls will be clean and secure.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Request and response travel over H T T P.
Methods are verbs; codes report outcome.
REST uses resources, U R Ls, and is stateless.
requests makes Python A P I calls easy.
Task: call a public A P I and read two fields.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Every A P I call is a request and a response over H T T P. The method is the verb, and the status code tells you the outcome. REST organises data as resources with their own U R Ls and stays stateless. And the requests library makes calling A P Is from Python easy. Your task before the next lesson: call a free public A P I, print the status code, and pull two fields out of the Jason response. Great work, and I'll see you next time.
